name: Vantablack Media Subvocal Ghost Codec — 'The Murmur'
product_name: Vantablack Media Subvocal Ghost Codec — 'The Murmur'
description: The Murmur is a subvocal communication implant that intercepts pre-phonation muscle signals in the larynx, tongue, and soft palate — capturing intended speech before it becomes audible sound — and transmits the encoded signal via a low-power Vantablack proprietary mesh protocol. The system reads electromyographic signals from the speech musculature and reconstructs intended words with 96.3% accuracy at full calibration, transmitting them as encrypted audio to paired receivers. Communication is entirely silent: no movement of the lips, no breath, no whisper. To any observer, the user is simply standing still.

cultural_context: Vantablack Media originally developed the Murmur for their own embedded journalists and field producers working in conflict zones and corporate-controlled information blackouts — the ability to report silently was a survival tool before it was a product. When it entered the broader market, it found immediate adoption in the intelligence and criminal communities. In GLMZ's social fabric, spotting someone with a Murmur is nearly impossible, which has generated a paranoid urban folklore: that in any given negotiation or meeting, at least one person in the room is broadcasting everything. The implant has quietly eroded trust in private conversations citywide.

story_hooks: The crew discovers that a contact they've been meeting with for months has a Murmur — every conversation has been broadcast to an unknown third party. The question is who, and what they've done with it.

A Vantablack journalist surfaces with footage and subvocal recordings of a closed-door corporate meeting that should have been impossible to penetrate — someone inside the meeting had a Murmur, and they want out.

The party is hired to protect a negotiator who insists on using a Murmur to receive coaching — but the encrypted channel has been compromised, and the 'analyst' feeding advice is not who they claim to be.
A black-market firmware update for the Murmur promises 100% accuracy and extended range — users who installed it report hearing voices that don't belong to anyone in their paired network.
